articles.title: Canada's Clean Grid Has a Rainy-Day Problem
articles.dek: How excessive reliance on hydroelectricity can harm Canada's clean-energy transition
articles.body:
## Clean, But Not Under Pressure
Canada’s electricity sector has a genuine success story to tell. Since 2005, greenhouse gas emissions from electricity generation have fallen by 58%, the single largest sectoral reduction anywhere in the Canadian economy.<sup>1</sup> In a normal year, more than 80% of the power flowing through Canadian homes and factories comes from non-emitting sources.<sup>2</sup> By all accounts, there has been real progress.

But a key vulnerability has surfaced in the last few years. Far from being normal, 2023-2025 frequently saw water levels decline to the territory of droughts. This in itself is a significant problem for a country as dependent on hydropower as Canada.

For a country focused on transitioning to clean energy, the problem is even worse because hydro shortfalls today are being met by a rise in fossil fuel generation. What’s more concerning is that this dynamic threatens to become a routine aspect of the electricity grid. Not a rare last resort, but a systemic response that pushes a few steps back for all the steps taken forward.

![British Columbia’s Comox Dam during a late 2022 drought. Source: https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/b-c-hydro-looks-to-protect-fish-as-drought-leaves-some-reservoirs-at-record-low-levels-1.6614626](data:image/jpeg;base64, "w=100")

## What Happens When It Doesn’t Rain
Hydro accounts for nearly 60% of national electricity generation. In provinces like British Columbia and Manitoba, its share climbs well above 90%.<sup>3</sup> To say that hydropower has been the bedrock of Canada’s clean electricity story would thus be an understatement.

But excessive reliance often has its drawbacks, as is the case here. The reservoirs behind hydro require a significant amount of rain and snowmelt. When this supply weakens, generation falls, and the grid has to find electricity somewhere else. In recent years, that somewhere else has largely been combustible fuels. In 2025, combustible fuel generation hit its highest level since Statistics Canada’s current data series began in 2016. At the same time, hydro’s share of total generation fell to a series low. Canada became a net electricity importer during multiple months of both 2024 and 2025, which is the first time this had occurred in the current series.<sup>4</sup>

![All values are in Terwatt-hours (TWh). Source: Statistics Canada, Table 25-10-0015-01](data:image/png;base64, "w=100 h=250")

The provincial picture suggests that these trends may be the early expression of a structural weakness rather than anomalies. Amid BC Hydro’s recent generation deficits, the province covered roughly a quarter of its electricity demand through imports at a cost of approximately $1.38 billion. A large share of these imports came from the United States and Alberta, where the grid ran at approximately 74.7% natural gas in 2024, with a carbon intensity more than four times the Canadian national average.<sup>5</sup> These emissions don’t show up in British Columbia’s official figures; provincial inventories only count what is generated within a province’s borders, so the carbon embedded in the imports is invisible in the accounting.

Manitoba, which generates about 97% of its electricity from hydro, tells a related story. To specifically address the issue of shortfalls, Manitoba Hydro has proposed a $3 billion natural gas facility at Brandon, which would strengthen the systemic link between hydropower and carbon emissions.<sup>6</sup> Both BC and Manitoba are responding to a real, common problem, but both approaches undermine the commitment to a clean grid. While one province is already reaching for high-carbon imports when hydro wavers, the other is preparing to generate high-carbon fuel itself.

## The Assumption of Abundance
The deeper issue is not that hydro is unreliable in an absolute sense. Over a long enough period, Canadian watersheds are productive and the generation record is strong. The issue is that the grid was designed around the assumption of hydro abundance, which is why it currently has very little clean energy to fall back on when that abundance runs short.
This creates an awkward reality at the heart of Canada’s clean electricity story: the grid’s low-emissions record is partly contingent on the weather. In dry years, the system quietly becomes more carbon-intensive because the backup capacity that exists is largely fossil-based.

Future developments can worsen this problem. The years 2023 and 2025 both featured significant drought conditions alongside some of the lowest hydro generation levels recorded in Canada.<sup>4</sup> Moreover, drought-like conditions have been present since even before 2023,<sup>11</sup> making the last few years remarkably unrelenting. This might signal a lasting, long-term shift in precipitation driven by climate change, as some BC Hydro officials believe.<sup>11</sup> If the pattern holds, it would necessitate a fundamental change in the assumptions tied to hydropower in grid planning.

The second concern, electrification, is a more concrete development. Canada’s federal government has committed to a net-zero electricity grid by 2050 and set binding emissions limits on generating units beginning in 2035.<sup>7</sup> It is peculiar to talk about electrification in this context because, in many ways, it is quite key to Canada’s broader clean-energy transition. But the push from fossil fuel-driven structures to electric ones naturally raises the demand for electricity, and therein lies an issue.

The Canada Energy Regulator projects electricity demand will grow between 26% and 44% by 2050 relative to 2023 levels.<sup>8 </sup>More demand on the same grid means more exposure to the same vulnerability. As total grid load grows with electrification and outpaces the increase in hydro capacity, the grid becomes more sensitive to droughts, even those of the same intensity as today. As a result, it requires an earlier intervention from other sources, and as it stands today, these other sources consist largely of fossil fuels. The takeaway, therefore, is not that electrification is the wrong strategy. It is that electrification might arrive before the system needed to support it sustainably.

## Toward a Grid That Remains Clean Even Under Pressure
This is not an argument against electrification or hydro. It is an argument for being honest about the limitations brought about by an excessive reliance on hydro, and for developing measures that ensure that energy supply remains clean even when hydro is strained.

How do you begin solving this problem? The future-oriented steps are expanding the storage capacity of wind and solar, both of which are already promising but intermittent in their current state, and expanding clean yet relatively under-developed sources like geothermal energy.<sup>9</sup> But there is also a key issue that can be tackled more immediately: provincial fragmentation. At present, Canada operates three largely separate regional grids — Western, Eastern, and Québec — with limited east-west interconnection, and provinces trade more electricity with US states than with each other. But a grid with interprovincial transmission could allow clean surplus generation in one region to cover deficits in another. After all, a drought affecting British Columbia’s reservoirs may not always affect Quebec’s or Manitoba’s to the same extent in the same year. Moreover, provinces like New Brunswick and Ontario (with its nuclear plants) can supply clean energy from sources other than hydro, ensuring that Canada’s grid is not singularly vulnerable to the difficulties faced by just one source.<sup>10</sup>


![Electricity transmission lines south of Chesley, On. Source: https://www.theglobeandmail.com/business/article-why-provinces-are-ramping-up-transmission-line-infrastructure/](data:image/jpeg;base64, "w=100")

Canada’s electricity sector has achieved something genuinely worth building on. The question now is whether the planning behind the transition is honest about the conditions under which the current approach holds, and the conditions under which it doesn’t. Acknowledging the gap clearly is the first step toward closing it.

articles.title: Medical Tourism in Istanbul: Why International Patients Choose Turkey for Treatment
articles.body:
Over the past decade, medical tourism in Istanbul has quietly transformed from a niche travel trend into a massive global industry. Walk through Istanbul Airport on any given day, and you will see international patients flying in from the UK, Europe, the Gulf, and North America, seeking everything from Hollywood-smile makeovers to world-class specialized surgeries.

Turkey wasn't always a global leader in medical tourism. In 2015, around 429,000 foreign patients came to the country for treatment. Fast forward to 2024, and that number skyrocketed to 1.5 million patients, bringing in nearly $3 billion in revenue according to Turkey's official health tourism agency, USHAŞ.<sup>1</sup>

Much of that activity is concentrated in Istanbul. The city combines internationally accredited private hospitals, strong global flight connections from Europe and Asia, and a healthcare system that has increasingly adapted itself around foreign patients. For people considering treatment abroad, Istanbul tends to come up early in the research process and usually persists as the final choice.

## Why Istanbul Is a Leading Medical Tourism Destination
### Accredited Hospitals With International Patient Services
One of the biggest reasons patients choose Istanbul is the sheer scale of its private healthcare sector.

Turkey hosts more than 40 JCI-accredited hospitals, and more than half of them are in Istanbul. JCI accreditation is a globally recognized quality standard, corroborating the quality of Istanbul's top clinics.<sup>2</sup>
The major accredited hospital groups in Istanbul include Acıbadem, which operates a network of 24 hospitals and 16 medical centers across Turkey,<sup>3</sup> as well as Memorial, Florence Nightingale, and the American Hospital. These institutions create comprehensive service packages for international patients, featuring multilingual staff, dedicated international patient departments, and coordinators who guide patients through scheduling, transfers, and recovery planning.

Istanbul's flight connections reinforce this convenience: the city is within a four-hour flight of approximately 57 countries,<sup>4</sup> with Istanbul Airport itself connecting to over 330 destinations worldwide.<sup>5</sup> Most international patients can arrive on a direct or single-connection flight, which makes the logistics of getting here, and of returning for any follow-up, quite manageable.

### Competitive Healthcare Pricing
Turkey's private healthcare is significantly cheaper than equivalent treatment in the US or UK. The medical tourism research firm Patients Beyond Borders estimates savings against US and UK prices at around 50 to 65 percent across procedures.<sup>6</sup>

To put that in concrete terms: a hair transplant procedure that costs nearly £6,000 in the UK typically runs around £1,860 in Istanbul.<sup>7</sup> A rhinoplasty that costs $7,500 to $12,500 in the US in surgeon fees alone runs $3,300 to $4,500 in Istanbul, all-inclusive.<sup>8</sup><sup>10</sup>

That price gap does not stem from lower quality. It stems from several structural factors, including lower operating costs, currency differences, and long-term government investment in medical tourism infrastructure.<sup>12</sup>
Turkey trains physicians across 128 accredited medical faculties, with many leading specialists also bringing international experience from respected institutions in Germany, UK, and the US.<sup>11</sup> At leading clinics in Istanbul, affordability is therefore balanced with excellence.

### Logistics Designed Around International Patients
One reason behind the rise of medical tourism in Istanbul is that the process has become highly streamlined.

HealthTürkiye, the official government portal, helps international patients connect with accredited facilities and arrange accommodations, airport transfers, and visa guidance.<sup>13</sup> Clinics treating foreign patients are required to hold a Ministry of Health International Health Tourism Authorization Certificate, which sets baseline standards for those operating within the regulated sector.<sup>13</sup>

In practice, many clinics operate almost like full-service international coordinators. Patients typically send photographs, scans, or medical records before traveling. Clinics review the information remotely, confirm candidacy for treatment, and outline pricing before the patient even books a flight.

The result is that most patient journeys begin weeks before arrival. Clinics ask for medical records or photographs upfront and use them to confirm a treatment plan remotely, so patients usually arrive knowing exactly what is scheduled and what the package covers.

## Common Procedures and Specialties in Istanbul
### Hair Transplants
Turkey is one of the world's leading destinations for hair transplant procedures by volume. The Turkish Health Tourism Association has estimated that roughly one million foreign patients traveled to Turkey for hair transplants in a single year.<sup>12</sup> That kind of volume directly contributes to surgeon expertise: practitioners here perform at a scale that simply isn't possible in lower-volume markets.

At the leading end of the market, hair restoration clinics in Istanbul operate within JCI-accredited hospitals such as Memorial and Acıbadem. These are the same facilities that are built to handle the most complex surgical procedures, and that have surgeons with rigorous specializations in their domains.

Pricing is another obvious draw. A 2,500-graft FUE procedure averages around $2,500 in Turkey, compared to roughly £6,000 in the UK and $13,610 in the US.<sup>14</sup> DHI, the more precision-intensive technique, runs $2,500 to $4,500 in Istanbul versus an average of $20,000 (range $16,000 to $24,000) in the US.<sup>15</sup>

Istanbul packages for such procedures also typically bundle in hotel accommodation, airport transfers, medication, and aftercare support, which are usually billed separately in other markets.

### Cosmetic and Plastic Surgery
Istanbul's surgeons are widely recognized for rhinoplasty, with a strong reputation for natural-looking results. A primary rhinoplasty is commonly advertised at €2,900 to €4,000 all-inclusive in Istanbul,<sup>8</sup> against £4,000 to £7,000 in the UK<sup>9</sup> and US surgeon fees alone of $7,500 to $12,500.<sup>10</sup>

Turkey has also become a major destination for cosmetic surgery in general. The International Society of Aesthetic Plastic Surgery (ISAPS) reported in its 2022 Global Survey that Turkey is among the four countries seeing the highest proportion of foreign patients for aesthetic surgery, which highlights overall demand for Turkish cosmetic procedures.<sup>16</sup>

Other commonly sought procedures include breast augmentation, abdominoplasty, blepharoplasty, and liposuction, each offering a similar combination of affordability and surgical experience.

### Dental Treatment
Istanbul is also one of the most popular dental tourism destinations in the world, with competitive pricing across most common procedures. A single porcelain veneer runs roughly £150 to £300 in Turkey,<sup>17</sup> versus £500 to £975 in the UK.<sup>18</sup> Dental implants show a similar pattern, priced at typically £330 to £825 per implant in Turkey,<sup>19</sup> compared with £1,800 to £4,500 in the UK.<sup>20</sup>

For patients requiring multiple veneers or full-mouth restoration work, the overall savings can remain substantial even after flights and accommodation are included.

Most dental patients stay five to seven days for veneers and three to five days for implant work. Since many procedures involve a preparatory appointment followed by a fitting, a multi-day stay is often a clinical requirement rather than just a recommendation.

## The Patient Experience in Istanbul
Most of the practical coordination happens before you land. After the remote consultation, clinics handle airport pickup and arrange accommodation close to the facility.

At Acıbadem, dedicated Health Point lounges at both Istanbul Airport and Sabiha Gökçen Airport receive arriving patients, provide free transfers to the hotel or hospital, and offer a waiting area before the first appointment.<sup>21</sup> Memorial Hospital has a similarly structured international patient program, with coordinators handling everything from treatment planning to discharge paperwork.<sup>22</sup>

Istanbul's major private hospitals are concentrated in districts like Şişli, Beşiktaş, and Ataşehir. Staying near one's clinic simplifies the early recovery days, particularly given the city's traffic. Clinics schedule follow-up appointments before discharge and provide aftercare instructions and medication, ensuring that patient experience remains smooth through comprehensive service.

## Before You Choose an Istanbul Clinic
### Check Accreditation
JCI accreditation is the most reliable quality indicator and is verifiable through the Joint Commission International's public directory.<sup>2</sup> The Turkish Ministry of Health's list of authorized health tourism providers is also publicly accessible.<sup>13</sup> For major procedures, choosing a JCI-accredited facility is worth prioritizing.

### Verify Your Surgeon
Ask directly about the surgeon's credentials, training, and procedure volume. Online reviews and promotional content are plentiful in this market, but they should not substitute for direct verification. Also confirm the clinic's policy for follow-up care once you return home.

### Plan Your Recovery Honestly
One of the most common mistakes medical tourists make is underestimating recovery time.
Flying home too soon is one of the leading causes of post-surgical complications in medical tourists. UK guidance from the NHS recommends waiting at least five to seven days before flying after procedures such as breast surgery or liposuction, and seven to ten days after facial cosmetic procedures or abdominoplasty.<sup>23</sup>

Patients should build the recovery window into their schedule from the start before booking flights.

## The Bottom Line
Istanbul has real infrastructure behind its reputation. Its accredited hospitals and experienced specialists fuel a system that has become a leader in both quality and affordability. For foreign patients, cost savings are substantial, and the quality at the top end of the market is globally competitive.

Getting a good outcome, however, still requires patients to be careful. Alongside accredited clinics, Istanbul also has an informal healthcare market that shows far more variation in its standards of care and outcomes. The takeaway is simple: check the accreditation, verify the surgeon, and plan the recovery honestly. By following these steps, one can secure outcomes that outpace most alternatives.
